text: Jean is with men, then with Laura, and the film refuses to treat that sequence as a discovery that ends in an answer. Cyril Collard gives the arrangement two full hours and withholds the vocabulary that would tidy it: Samy is not a phase, Laura is not a cure, and the crisis Jean is inside of is not the sort a decision settles. A French film of 1992 could have taken this premise in either direction, as a plea or as a caution, and this one accepts neither commission. What is at stake is smaller and harder than a choice between two people. It is whether a man who wants what he wants can be honest at the speed his life is running. Two hours is a long time to spend with someone who will not simplify himself, which is exactly the reason to spend it.

One generation cuts a road through the taiga toward a star on the horizon. The next sets about building communism. The third drills for oil. The village they work from is small enough that the country forgot it was there, and Andrei Konchalovsky keeps returning to it across eight decades and 275 minutes, a length that turns method into argument. Whatever is asked of that ground, the asking never stops. His structure is generational rather than dramatic, so a man can age out of importance and hand the century to whoever comes next without ceremony. War, history and romance are all in the description, and the century supplies each of them in turn. Cannes gave it the Grand Prix. Each generation arrives certain that it has located the land of happiness and means to hand it over, and the village is where that intention keeps landing.

Two actors play eighteen Yorkshire villagers, and a cigarette lit or not lit at one moment decides which lives they get. Alain Resnais built the film as a machine with a switch in it: the branch point is trivial, one cigarette, and the consequences run to marriages, jobs, decades. Across 280 minutes the same juncture is run again with different outcomes, so the pleasure is comparative rather than narrative, two versions of a person held at once while the small divergence compounds. It is also a comedy of English provincial manners conducted entirely in French, which lays a second translation over a work already made of alternatives. The Césars for Best Film and Best Actress went to it, as did the Louis Delluc Prize. Nothing in it depends on suspense. Everything depends on remembering what happened the last time.

In 1931 Swedish soldiers fired on demonstrating workers in the sawmill district of Ådalen. Bo Widerberg came back to it thirty-eight years later, and the film he made spends much of its length away from the confrontation: on households where a strike is a domestic fact before it is a political one, on a love story the dispute keeps intruding into, on days whose direction none of the people living them can see. It is a history and a romance at once. The romance is the instrument; it sets the cost at the size of a family rather than a movement. The Grand Prix at Cannes went to it, and Sweden sent it to the Academy Awards as its international entry. Everything in the 114 minutes proceeds at the pace of people who assume there will be a next week.

Fatima lives in France with two teenage daughters she can barely talk to. She was born in Algeria; the girls were formed by the country she moved to, and the gap between those facts runs through language and through everything language happens to be carrying. Philippe Faucon takes 79 minutes for it, a decision rather than a shortfall, since the compression keeps the film out of saga territory and puts the weight on ordinary exchanges, on what gets said at the speed of a household and what gets abandoned mid-sentence. The César for Best Film and for Best Actress came to it, along with the Louis Delluc Prize. What stands to be lost is not the household. It is the daughters' access to who their mother is, which erodes without any incident to mark it and cannot be restored by an argument.

The wax museum is of ancient Rome, and it stands in New York. Marco Ferreri drops an electrotechnician named Lafayette into that city and surrounds him with people running incompatible programs: a museum director of grandiose designs, a solitary Italian anarchist, a company of feminist actresses, one of whom, Angelica, falls for him. He adopts a small chimpanzee, the only party to the arrangement with no position to advance. Produced in France, performed in Italian, set in an America the film treats as already historical, it is a comedy in the sense that every situation is absurd and nobody inside one is joking. Cannes gave it the Grand Prix. Ferreri works at the scale of farce and the temperature of a quarrel, and nothing in the setup was assembled in order to resolve.

Juli returns to Budapest from the Soviet Union with her parents gone and a set of memories she has no one left to check against. Márta Mészáros films it as testimony rather than reminiscence. The account is being kept for children, people who were not present and will have to take somebody's word for it. Her aunt Magda becomes her adoptive mother, which settles the legal question and none of the others. Stalin's oppression operates here as air pressure rather than subject, setting what can be said aloud in an apartment and what has to be carried instead. Hungary in 1984, going back to those years on purpose; Cannes answered with the Grand Prix. What the film watches most closely is a girl working out whom to believe, and how much of that decision she is allowed to show.

A young Polish woman crosses Europe after a man who has gone to Rome to be rid of a previous wife. What she meets instead is a series of arrangements: every man she encounters has a scheme already running, and her arrival is treated as material for it. Walerian Borowczyk, working in Poland in 1975, gives this 130 minutes, long enough for the pattern to stop reading as misfortune and start reading as design. The film is classed as drama and romance, and it turns the second word against itself, since the language of devotion is available to anyone in the story who wants something and costs nothing to speak. The tragedies dealt out along the way are not accidents of travel. They are what happens when a woman's own purpose is the one thing nobody around her has any use for.

An old man says the birds taught him to fly, and a young drifter with nowhere in particular to be stays on to find out what that means. Alain Tanner has the thing classed as drama and fantasy at once, and the pairing is the whole tension: the claim is either a delusion being humored or an apprenticeship being offered, and the film declines to settle which in advance. Two people and one assertion is a severe basis for 107 minutes, so everything rests on how the younger man chooses to take the older one. It carried the Grand Prix at Cannes. Whatever the old man turns out to be, he is filmed as a person with a project rather than as a lesson. What is being risked is not sanity but time, years handed over to somebody else's proposition on no security beyond the way he states it.

Henri Rainier is called into his director's office at the bank and told, in the courteous vocabulary institutions keep for the purpose, that the loss is his. He has the glamorous wife, the two daughters, the well-paid position; then a scandal breaks, needs a name attached to it, and his is the one within reach. What follows is not a thriller of vaults and pursuit but an inquiry run from the wrong side of a resignation, by a man whose one remaining asset is that he knows how the paperwork moves. France, 1978. The Césars for Best Film, Best Director and Best Editing went to it, the editing prize the least decorative of the three, since a story built from meetings and denials lives in the cut. What stands to be lost is not the money, which was never his, but the assumption that a record exists somewhere that will say what happened.

Miho and Toshio stay married, and that is the hard part: the marriage is what they fight with rather than what they are fighting over. Kōhei Oguri gives the two of them 115 minutes and no exit. The children, the house, the daily machinery of a middle-aged household are all placed on the table as stakes, and neither party will concede the room. The film took the Grand Prix at Cannes, and Japan sent it to the Academy Awards as its international entry. What is unusual is the patience. A duel of this kind is normally compressed into a few scenes of shouting; here it is given the duration of a siege, with the household's routine obligations continuing throughout. Nothing is settled by argument, and the arguing does not stop.

A librarian, single by conviction, has decided she will not be a mother; a six-year-old is meanwhile looking for a place in a family still being assembled. Carine Tardieu sets a young single father between those two positions and gives him the harder assignment: not the raising, which he is already doing, but finding the strength to love, treated here as a capacity that can run low rather than a feeling that arrives. Belgian-produced and played in French, it runs 106 minutes and stays inside the domestic register the whole way. The interest is in how a household forms when nobody involved has agreed to the word family, what gets shared first, who is permitted to be tired, which obligations show up before the feelings that would justify them. None of the three chose the others. None of them is free of the others either.

A pilot is made to be judged rather than watched, which is a strange demand to put on six minutes of animation. This one comes out of Peter Bagge's comic book series, and the transfer sets a specific problem. A comic's timing belongs to the reader, who decides how fast the eye moves down a page, while animation takes that control back and hands it to a clock. What survives such a move is usually manner rather than incident, a way of drawing a face, a rhythm of speech, and manner is precisely what an adaptation of a comic has to carry or abandon. Steve Loter directs, in 1995, with the entire case to be made before the six minutes are used up: a world, a voice, and a reason to continue, established at once and then stopped.

A documentary with a script, in which the people interviewed are primary school pupils and the subject is addiction. Marek Koterski's thirteen minutes, made in Poland in 1982, put pressure on the first of those words. The writing is acknowledged rather than concealed, which is a more honest position than it looks, since a child answering an adult's question about drugs is performing either way. The running time announces the purpose, since a film this size is cut to fit inside a class period and to do a class period's work, name a cause and warn against an effect. What complicates the job is the casting. The pupils on screen supply the material and the class that would be shown the film supplies the audience, and they are the same children, being taught by a version of themselves that somebody else wrote.
